resolved.title: Astral Projection: Adventures Beyond the Body William Buhlman
resolved.description:
The Astral Projecting Podcast

I had my first OBE (Out of Body Experience) about 30 years ago, back when I was in my early 20's. At first, I was terrified by the whole experience. My OBE was brought on, ironically, by my wife having her own Out-of-body experience on the same night.

She had just left her body and was startled by the fact that she was flying around in the house, up near the ceiling and was able to pass through walls and doors in the house.

She also was able to call up her 3-year-old son who was sleeping in another room in the house. He then was up with her (in the Astral body) and flying around with her in the house!

After all the talk and conversation of this whole experience that night, I too later found myself leaving my body, as well as in a state of total paralysis! This totally scared me, as I had no idea what was going on. I honestly thought I was having a stroke, or maybe even dying. After all - Why else would my Spirit be leaving my body and floating away? Why else was my physical body totally paralyzed, and, when I tried to yell out for help, no words came out?

Fast forward 30+ years to today and I find myself reading "Adventures Beyond the Body: How to Experience Out-of-Body Travel: Proving Your Immortality Through Out-of-Body" by William Buhlman

I'm now 100% convinced that the experience I had all those years ago was not only something to not be afraid of, but rather, something Millions of people do each year, AND something we should do and can do with amazing benefits and results.

After reading William Buhlman's book, I'm not only excited about Astral Projection, but am now starting this new podcast to talk about the benefits of Astral Projecting, how we can do it, why we should do it, and what we can expect when we do it.

I'm talking with real people about their own real Astral Projection experiences (both good and bad) and will be interviewing experts, Doctors and book authors who write about Astral Projecting, NDE, OBE and the Afterlife.

We all know about life and death, yet, as natural as death is, and as inevitable as it is, many of us fear death due to the unknown. None of us have much certainty about what happens to us when we die. This is tragic, as the answers are right there in front of us and, as William Buhlman outlines in his book "Adventures Beyond the Body", we can have proof of the afterlife now. 

We can prove beyond a shadow of a doubt that we are actually eternal beings living in a temporary physical body (vehicle) which is something we can leave as and when we choose. He explains that we don't need to wait until we die to have an experience in the "non-physical" world, and in so doing, we can connect with our true selves at a much higher level, get a glimpse of what our life is all about, and more importantly, to get a sense of where we will be going once we die. (our physical body dies since our Soul never does)

In this episode, I talk a little bit about the core concepts I have taken from the book, as well as my own out-of-body experience and how I came to be on this new and exciting journey of Astral Projection.

William Buhlman's forty years of extensive personal out-of-body explorations give him a unique and thought provoking insight into this subject. His first book, Adventures beyond the Body chronicles his personal journey of self-discovery through out-of-body travel, and provides the reader with the preparation and techniques that can be used for their own adventure.

He has conducted an international out-of-body experience survey that includes over 16,000 participants from forty-two countries. The provocative results of this survey are presented in his book, The Secret of the Soul. This cutting edge book explores the unique opportunities for personal growth and profound spiritual awakenings that are reported during out-of-body experiences.

His third book is titled Adventures in the Afterlife. William was inspired to explore the afterlife a result of his confrontation with mortality following a cancer diagnosis in 2011. His lucid dreams and out of body experiences during his treatment and recovery provided mind bending visions that were so illuminating that he felt compelled to journal his experience. Insights that are provided in this book will assist the reader to navigate the many thought responsive environments in the afterlife.

William's book, Higher Self Now!, reflects on the actions we can take today to enhance our transition from a physical environment to the non physical world. With his wife, Susan, William wrote this book with the deep desire to help inform readers about the continuing reality of our existence and all that it implies. As a lifelong explorer through self-induced out-of-body experiences and meditation, he has written Part One of this book, which explores our opportunities for spiritual awakening, the multidimensional continuum of consciousness and the journey of soul that continues through our life, death and beyond. As a hospice volunteer and a certified end-of-life doula, Susan has written Part Two, which examines the transition we call death, suggesting a new paradigm for assisting our loved ones—and ourselves—in making the transition experience an effective launch pad for a profound spiritual journey.

Over the past two decades William has developed an effective system to experience safe, self initiated out-of-body adventures. He conducts an in-depth 4 week online workshop titled, Adventures beyond the Body, Mastering the Out-of-Body Experience. This unique workshop provides the steps, intention and techniques designed for controlled out-of-body exploration. Each participant will experience a comprehensive array of proven OBE methods including the target technique, inner motion, visualization, chakra and energy body activation. In addition, hypnotic, shamanic and early morning methods will be practiced.

As a certified hypnotherapist, William incorporates various methods in his workshops to explore the profound nature of out-of-body experiences and the benefits of accelerated personal development. Through lectures, workshops and his books the author teaches the preparation and techniques of astral projection and spiritual exploration.

The author brings a refreshing look to how we can use out-of-body experiences to explore our spiritual identity and enhance our intellectual and physical lives. William is best known for his ability to teach people how to have profound spiritual adventures through the use of out-of-body experiences. In addition, he has developed an extensive series of audio and video programs that are designed to expand awareness and assist in the exploration of consciousness. William has appeared on numerous television and radio shows worldwide. William's books are currently available in ten languages.

resolved.description:
In this podcast, Michael Raduga, founder of REMspace and the Phase Research Center, delves into his extensive research and innovations in the realms of lucid dreaming, REM sleep, and sleep paralysis. He shares his personal journey from his first encounter with sleep paralysis at 16, through years of experimentation and development of new technologies, to relocating his work from Russia to California. Raduga discusses his efforts in creating devices to induce lucid dreams, control real-world technology via dreams, and enhance the intersection between the dream world and reality. Highlighting both his dedication and radical personal experiments, including self-neurosurgery to test brain stimulation during sleep, Raduga emphasizes the future potential of integrating lucid dreams with daily life and solving real-world problems, such as overcoming phobias.

resolved.title: EXAMINING FREE WILL - Susan Blackmore PHD #30
resolved.description:
Is our subjective experience of Free Will, supported by the experimental evidence? If the evidence shows that our experience is not accurate, how do we take moral responsibility for our actions? Why do meditators, who’re used to watching their thoughts arise and pass without identifying with them, find this data easier to integrate?

In this episode, we have the tough job of evaluating the experimental evidence for the existence of Free Will. The debate has raged for centuries in Philosophy, but now with advances in neuroscience and psychology experiments, we may have some actual physical evidence to examine, and its implications to reflect on. We’re going to discuss how most of those who accept this evidence have chosen to carry on as if it they still have Free Will, which sounds contradictory. Do the implications for personal moral responsibility require us to do that? We’re also going to get into meditation and Zen, as our guest today and another famous advocate of the illusion of free will, Sam Harris, are long term practitioners. It seems those who use some kind of mindfulness meditation, and hence are used to watching the way thoughts arise and pass without identifying with them, are less troubled by the idea that they may not have free will. What does all this mean for the reality of a ‘self’?

So who better to explain this mind boggling question than, our first returning guest, psychologist, author and visiting Professor at Plymouth University, Susan Blackmore. Best known for her books The Meme Machine, Zen and the Art of Consciousness, Consciousness: An Introduction, and Seeing Myself, Sue’s work spans across hundreds of publications in over 20 different languages, making huge contributions in the fields of psychology, memetics, religion, philosophy of mind, supernatural experience, and many other areas.

Andrew Holecek joins Rick for a wide-ranging conversation about meditation, dreaming, dying, and what it actually takes to integrate spiritual realization into everyday life. Andrew completed a traditional three-year Buddhist retreat under Chögyam Trungpa Rinpoche's lineage, and he draws on those years of practice along with decades of teaching to talk about the real shape of the path, including the parts that don't get talked about as much.

The discussion opens with the ethics of enlightenment and the difference between waking up and growing up, drawing on Ken Wilber's states-and-structures framework. Andrew is candid about the complications of crazy wisdom teachers, the importance of Sila (ethics) as the ground of practice, and why so many Western practitioners skip past it at their peril. He and Rick dig into the trap of absolutism, the tantric idea that obstacles are opportunities in disguise, and how to find the spiritual in the material rather than escaping into a pure-land bypass.

From there the conversation moves into Andrew's specialty: the nocturnal meditations. He walks through liminal dreaming, lucid dreaming, dream yoga, sleep yoga, and bardo yoga, explaining why the dream state is up to nine times more efficacious for transformation than waking practice, and how lucid dreaming naturally extends into lucid living and lucid dying. They cover the science of consciousness, the subtle body, collective consciousness and the Maharishi Effect, and what a truly realized practitioner looks like at the end of life.

Andrew is the author of six books including Dreams of Light, Dream Yoga, and Preparing to Die, and the founder of Nightclub and the Preparing to Die Institute.

“Lucidity is a code word for awareness.”

Lucid dreaming expert, author, “curiouist,” and integralist Andrew Holecek explains how lucid dreaming opens the door to a greatly expanded understanding of our minds, our perception of reality, and human potential altogether. If we consciously explore our night lives practicing dream yoga, we can learn how to discard our habits, purify our karma, and discover beyond a shadow of a doubt that we are co-creators of our experience. What we do in dream yoga is not limited to nighttime action; it weaves back into our daytime lives, and ultimately our experience of dying.

Andrew describes how dreams are a powerful way to discover emptiness and openness, and fall into reality—like falling into love—our primordial contraction cast away. Besides being a life-changing discourse on the incredible potential of dream yoga, Andrew Holecek’s cheerful, well-informed, easy way of talking and teaching about lucid dreaming—relating it also to the wisdom traditions, our sense of identity, and human evolution—makes this a real pleasure to listen to. In this interview, Tami Simon speaks with Andrew Holecek—interdisciplinary scholar, Tibetan Buddhist practitioner, and author of the new Sounds True book Total Eclipse of the Mind: Unleashing the Power of Darkness for Creativity, Healing, and Transformation—about the ancient practice of dark retreat: full immersion in complete, sealed darkness used by yogis for centuries to accelerate awakening, healing, and creative breakthrough.

After fifty years of meditation, psychedelic exploration, and completing a traditional three-year Tibetan retreat, Holecek calls dark retreat easily the most transformative practice he has ever done. This interview was recorded with both Tami and Andrew wearing blackout eye masks—making it one of the most experientially immersive episodes in Insights at the Edge history.

Together, they explore:
• What actually happens to the mind in extended darkness—and the neurological science behind why it's so transformative
• The descent of the mind through conscious, subconscious, and collective unconscious layers—and what waits at the bottom

• Why appearances don't matter in the dark—and why so many people emerge in tears, feeling safe and held for the first time
• How to bring the power of darkness into daily life: from sleep masks and gray retreat to dedicated dark rooms

Whether or not a full dark retreat is in your future, this interview offers a profound reframe of darkness—within and around you—that changes everything.

resolved.title: Is Reality Really Real? With Donald Hoffman
resolved.description:
Did evolution never give us the ability to see reality as it actually is? Neil deGrasse Tyson and co-hosts Chuck Nice and Gary O’Reilly sit down with cognitive scientist Donald Hoffman to explore what neuroscience, evolutionary game theory, and consciousness suggest about the nature of reality itself.

Is evolution the correct tool for tuning our senses to reality? Are our perceptions less like a window and more like a VR headset? We discuss the priorities of our perceptions and how it may not always be truth. We explore how psychedelics impact our perception of reality. Could hallucinogens show us a layer of reality we don’t otherwise see? Does the mind render things only when perceived, the way a video game only generates what's on screen? The team explores if we are in a simulation and how Donald doesn't think spacetime itself is fundamental.

Can consciousness be modeled? Donald breaks down how we have struggled to define consciousness and provide a theory for the observer. What is an observer, really? Chuck's ayahuasca encounters with higher-dimensional beings become surprisingly relevant, as we explore how to test for consistencies across individuals’ trips.  Could information passed to one user be received by another in a separate session? Doubtful, says Hoffman, but testable.

We explore the Matrix, both the movie and the mathematical, discussing how you could use math to understand the role of the observer. The episode closes on science, God, and Gödel. Does some of this verge on the spiritual? Have theologians approached Hoffman, hoping he's providing scientific grounding for a god?

Dr. Radin's original career track as a concert violinist shifted into science after earning a BSEE degree in electrical engineering, magna cum laude and with honors in physics, from the University of Massachusetts, Amherst, and then an MS in electrical engineering and a PhD in psychology from the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign. 

For a decade Dr. Radin worked on advanced R&D at AT&T Bell Laboratories and GTE Laboratories. For over three decades he has been engaged in research on the frontiers of consciousness. Dr. Radin is author or co-author of hundreds of scientific, technical, and popular articles, four dozen book chapters, and four best-selling books including The Conscious Universe (recipient of the Scientific and Medical Network’s 1997 book award), Entangled Minds, Supernormal (recipient of the 2014 Silver Nautilus Book Award), and Real Magic. Dr. Radin’s books have been translated into over a dozen languages.

Dr. Radin’s 100+ academic articles appear in peer-reviewed journals ranging from Foundations of Physics and Physics Essays to Psychological Bulletin, Psychology of Consciousness, and Frontiers in Human Neuroscience. He is a sought-after speaker, and has given over 600 talks for prestigious schools, government, military, business, scientific, and other groups around the world.

resolved.title: Rapid Responses to Auditory Frequency Change -  from Brain to Action - Amos Boasson
resolved.description:
Rapid Responses to Auditory Frequency Change, Its Magnitude and Direction – from Brain to Action - Amos Boasson

https://www.unibw.de/socialbridges/socialbridges5talks/boasson

Amos David Boasson
agboas@gmail.com
Edmond and Lily Safra Center for Brain Sciences, The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Israel

Gal Vishne
gal.vishne@gmail.com
Edmond and Lily Safra Center for Brain Sciences, The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Israel

Leon Deouell
leon.deouell@mail.huji.ac.il
Edmond and Lily Safra Center for Brain Sciences, The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Israel
Department of Psychology, Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Israel

Roni Granot
ronigra@gmail.com
Department of Musicology, Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Israel

Auditory frequency change [FC] may convey to perceivers potentially crucial environmental cues, entailing immediate behavioral responses. Our research-line explores swift (albeit at times covert) effects of FC and its parameters on human motor action, and the junctions where this auditory information may be relayed into motor commands.
Previously (Boasson & Granot, 2019) we employed a finger-tapping task, monitoring negative mean asynchrony, muscle-action, and finger acceleration. Isochronous beeps (rate 4 Hz) were set in sequences presenting task-irrelevant increments/ decrements, in frequency/intensity. FC elicited augmented asynchrony, revealing 'melodic' asymmetry: yet more enhanced 'tap-earliness' followed Rise (thus no mere surprise effect). Physiological data detected Rise's effect-onset at ~160 ms post-FC; Fall impacted action significantly later. Diverging response-patterns to FC vs Intensity Change suggested domain-specificity.

Focusing on auditory-to-motor mediation, the present study explored FC effects on both behavioral and neural activity at a motor task evoked in response to FCs presented at random time intervals (instead of activity pre-planned by synchronizing to a regularly-paced auditory input, as in the tapping paradigm).

Detailed FC detection early up the auditory pathways elicited (in musicians) ultra-early action. Hence, early ‘decisions’, based on finely-processed information, yield motor commands at early primary auditory cortex levels, perhaps even sub-cortically. Upcoming, testing non-musicians could further our insight.
Bewildering our concept of consciousness threshold, bottom-up and top-down processes meet at 'low' levels, activating auditory-to-motor relays. Enabling rapid responses to FC information, such primal routes may act regularly, though covertly, possibly forming motoric 'low-level' facets of auditory perception, both generally and in realms focusing on distilled FC, as Music.

Boasson, A., & Granot, R. (2019). Short Latency Effects of Auditory Frequency Change on Human Motor Behavior. Auditory Perception & Cognition, 2(1-2), 98-128.

resolved.title: Using Meditation to Focus, View Consciousness & Expand Your Mind | Dr. Sam Harris
resolved.description:
My guest is Sam Harris, Ph.D. Sam earned his bachelor’s degree in philosophy from Stanford University and his doctorate (Ph.D.) in neuroscience from the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA). He is the author of multiple best-selling books and is a world-renowned public-facing intellectual on meditation, consciousness, free will, psychedelics and neuroscience. He is also the creator of Waking Up and the host of the Making Sense podcast. In this episode, we discuss meditation as a route to understanding “the self” and experiencing consciousness, not just changing one’s conscious state. Sam describes several meditation techniques and their benefits, including how meditation fundamentally changes our worldview and how it can be merged seamlessly into daily life. It can help us overcome universal challenges such as distractibility and persistent internal dialogue (“chatter”) to allow for deep contentment and pervasive shifts in our awareness, all while acknowledging the more immediate stress-lowering and memory-improving effects of meditation. We also discuss the therapeutic use of psychedelics and the mechanistic similarities between the benefits of a psychedelic journey and long-term meditation practices. And we discuss the rationale behind Sam’s recent decision to close his social media (Twitter) account. This episode should interest anyone wanting to learn more about the higher-order functions of the brain, the brain-body connection, consciousness and, of course, meditation and why and how to meditate for maximum benefit.

"Why is it that some people are more vulnerable to life's slings and arrows and others more resilient?" In this eye-opening talk, Richard Davidson discusses how mindfulness can improve well-being and outlines strategies to boost four components of a healthy mind: awareness, connection, insight, and purpose. 

Richard Davidson is researching how mindfulness changes the emotional life of our brains and what we know about people's brains of individuals showing more resilience than others. Davidson is Wiliam James and Vilas professor of psychology and psychiatry at the University of Wisconsin-Madison as well as founder and director of the Center for Healthy Minds. His research is focused on the neural bases of emotion and emotional style and methods to promote human flourishing, including meditation and related contemplative practices. #Neuroscience #Wellbeing #MentalHealth Richard Davidson is Research Professor of Psychology and Psychiatry and Founder & Director of the Center for Healthy Minds, University of Wisconsin-Madison.Davidson’s research is focused on the neural bases of emotion and emotional style and methods to promote human flourishing including meditation and related contemplative practices.   He has published more than 400 articles and is the co-author of “The Emotional Life of Your Brain” and “Altered Traits: Science Reveals How Meditation Changes Your Mind, Brain, and Body”, both published by Penguin. Davidson has been recognized for his research through various awards, such as a National Institute of Mental Health Research Scientist Award and an  Established Investigator Award from the National Alliance for Research in Schizophrenia and Affective Disorders (NARSAD). Davidson received his Ph.D. from Harvard University in Psychology and has been teaching psychology and psychiatry at the University of Wisconsin-Madison since 1984. resolved.title: Altered States of Consciousness with Charles T. Tart
resolved.uploader: New Thinking Allowed with Jeffrey Mishlove
resolved.channel: New Thinking Allowed with Jeffrey Mishlove
resolved.description:
Charles T. Tart, PhD, is emeritus professor of psychology at the University of California, Davis, as well as the Institute of Transpersonal Psychology. He is a past-president of the Parapsychological Association. He has published over 100 scientific papers in parapsychology. He is editor of several anthologies including Altered States of Consciousness, Transpersonal Psychologies, Mind at Large, and Body Mind Spirit: Exploring the Parapsychology of Spirituality. Books that he has authored include Psi: Scientific Studies in the Psychic Realm, States of Consciousness, The End of Materialism, Learning to Use Extrasensory Perception, On Being Stoned, Waking Up: Overcoming the Obstacles to Human Potential, and Open Mind – Discriminating Mind.

Here he discusses a number of altered states including marijuana intoxication, dreaming, hypnosis, and out-of-body experiences. He describes his concept of “state specific research” using lucid dreaming as a clear example. Excerpts from the film, Altered States, with actor William Hurt are shown as they refer to Tart and his work. He also reviews the significance of altered states of consciousness for psychology in general as well as for our understanding of spirituality and the soul. He suggests that different states of consciousness are like different tools, each with unique capabilities.

New Thinking Allowed host, Jeffrey Mishlove, PhD, is author of The Roots of Consciousness, Psi Development Systems, and The PK Man. Between 1986 and 2002 he hosted and co-produced the original Thinking Allowed public television series. He is the recipient of the only doctoral diploma in "parapsychology" ever awarded by an accredited university (University of California, Berkeley, 1980). He is past-vice-president of the Association for Humanistic Psychology, and is the recipient of the Pathfinder Award from that association for his contributions to the study of consciousness. 

(Recorded on November 10, 2016)

resolved.title: Jim Fadiman on "Cultural Implications of Altered State of Consciousness"
resolved.description:
One cannot speak long about consciousness without eventually having to grapple with altered states of consciousness brought on by physical exertion, sensory privation, fasting, meditation, many spiritual practices, especially drumming, and the ingestion of psychedelic substances. Well before recorded history human beings were deliberately inducing such states for knowledge, healing, maybe even for pleasure. Evidence from Paleolithic art, pre-Columbian art, aboriginal Australian art and myths, as well as from the earliest remarkably similar worldwide shamanistic practices, all indicate that such states were highly valued in otherwise dissimilar cultures. Looking at history through the lens of altered states leads to a serious revaluation of the revelations of Zoroaster, Moses, Jesus, Buddha and Mohammed as well as the 1500 years of the Eleusinian mysteries that collectively define much of what we call civilization. When we then look into the lives and writing of mystics in each tradition, we may be dealing with the aftereffects of such states on cognition, perception and belief. Fast forward to the 1960s. Individuals, acting on a revised worldview after using psychedelics, in part fueled the social unrest, especially in the United States, that fostered the ecology movement, women’s liberation, civil rights and the anti-war movement as well as the so-called New Age phenomenon. These substances remain widely available, even after being declared illegal forty years ago. The exact amount of psychedelic use worldwide is unknown, but it is most prevalent in the more highly educated and highly mobile groups in many countries. In short, we are in an era where the very fabric of consciousness itself is under scrutiny, academically and in the laboratory, but perhaps more importantly through widespread individual experiences, which, for many, shatter the cultural consensus and question the scientific one. The implications of ongoing widespread use will be considered.

James Fadiman (Ph.D. in psychology, Stanford) was involved in the beginnings of experimental research on the effects of psychedelics on mind and consciousness in the 1960s. When no longer allowed to do psychedelic research, he held a variety of jobs including teaching (San Francisco State, Brandeis, and Stanford) management consulting, training, counselling, and editorial positions. For the past three decades, he has been a Professor at the Institute of Transpersonal Psychology (now Sofia University), which he co-founded. He has given workshops on three continents, published textbooks, professional books, a self-help book, a novel, and a series of videos about drugs for National Public Television. His books have been published in eight languages. He has been featured in a National Geographic documentary and had three solo shows of his nature photography.  Recently he has been involved in researching spiritual, therapeutic and creative states of consciousness, and his books include Personality and Personal Growth (now in its 2012, 7th Edition), Essential Sufism (with Robert Frager), 1997, and The Psychedelic Explorer’s Guide: Safe, Therapeutic, and Sacred Journeys, 2011. See http://www.jamesfadiman.com/

Wouter explains how he landed a position as The University of Amsterdam chair of Hermeticism, and then began to “map” the field of esoterism, the two poles of his academic interests are Hermeticism and esotericism. Hanegraaff is Professor of History of Hermetic Philosophy and Related Currents at the University of Amsterdam, the Netherlands, a member of the Royal Dutch Academy of Arts and Sciences, as well as past President and now honorary member of the European Society for the Study of Western Esotericism. Alongside numerous articles, he is the author of New Age Religion and Western Culture: Esotericism in the Mirror of Secular Thought (Leiden 1996/Albany 1998); Lodovico Lazzarelli (1447-1500): The Hermetic Writings and Related Documents (Tempe 2005; with Ruud M. Rare 195 Robert Monroe Interview. Astral Travel, OBE, Lucid Dreaming

Robert Monroe was a successful and distinguished business executive, dedicated family man, and noted pioneer in the investigation of human consciousness. He invented the Hemi-Sync® audio technology and founded The Monroe Institute®, a global organization dedicated to expanding the uses and understanding of consciousness.

Born in Indiana on October 30, 1915, to a college professor father and medical doctor mother and raised in Lexington, Kentucky, Robert Monroe was the third of four children.

After a childhood spent in Kentucky and Indiana, he attended Ohio State University. Upon graduating in 1937 with a BA in English, Monroe worked as a writer and director at two Ohio radio stations. Two years later he moved to New York and expanded his broadcasting career, producing and directing weekly radio programs and eventually forming his own radio production company. During the 1950s his company was producing 28 radio shows per month, including the popular Take a Number and Meet Your Match quiz shows. At this time Monroe became well known as a composer of music for radio, television, and motion pictures.

He also served as vice president and a member of the board of directors for the Mutual Broadcasting System network, was listed in Who's Who in America, and was publicized in magazine and newspaper articles on flying and radio production. Building on this success, Monroe's production company acquired several radio stations in North Carolina and Virginia and later moved into developing cable television systems.

In 1956 the firm set up a research and development division to study the effects of various sound patterns on human consciousness, including the feasibility of learning during sleep. Never one to ask others to do something he would not, Monroe often used himself as a test subject for this research. In 1958, a significant result emerged—Monroe began experiencing a state of consciousness separate and apart from the physical body. He described the state as an "out-of-body experience," the term popularized by Charles T. Tart, Ph.D. a leader in the area of consciousness studies. These spontaneous experiences altered the course of Monroe's life and the direction of his professional efforts.

While continuing his successful broadcasting activities, Monroe began to experiment with and research the expanded forms of consciousness that he was experiencing. He chronicled his early explorations with a reporter's objectivity and eye for detail in a groundbreaking book, Journeys Out of the Body, which was published in 1971. This public record of his out-of-body experiences in states beyond space, time, and death has comforted countless people who've encountered paranormal incidents. It also attracted the attention of academic researchers, medical practitioners, engineers, and other professionals.

Ever the pragmatic business leader, Monroe and a growing group of fellow researchers began to work on methods of inducing and controlling this and other forms of consciousness in a laboratory setting. This research led to the development of a noninvasive and easy-to-use enhanced binuarl beat audio guidance technology known as hemispheric synchronization or Hemi-Sync®. In 1974, the original research group was expanded to become The Monroe Institute, an organization dedicated to conducting seminars in the control and exploration of human consciousness. A year later, Monroe was issued the first of three patents for "Frequency Following Response" or FFR, which is part of the Hemi-Sync method of altering brain states through sound.

Throughout the next 20 years, Monroe continued to explore, research, and teach others about expanded states of human consciousness and practical methods of using them to enhance the experience of life. He developed a series of multi-day workshops that enable participants to personally access realms beyond physical time-space reality, built a campus for education and research, and created a portfolio of enhanced binaural beat audio exercises designed to focus attention, reduce stress, improve meditation, enhance sleep, and manage pain, among other applications.

In 1985 he wrote a second book, titled Far Journeys, which expanded upon his personal investigations of nonphysical reality. In 1994 he followed suit with a third book, Ultimate Journey, which explores basic truths about the meaning and purpose of life and what lies beyond the limits of our physical world. Monroe died in 1995, at the age of 79. His legacy continues today and has touched the lives of literally millions of people all around the world.

resolved.title: Cognitive Neuroscience of Mindfulness Meditation
resolved.description:
Google Tech Talks
February, 28 2008

ABSTRACT

Mindfulness meditation, one type of meditation technique, has been shown to
enhance emotional awareness and psychological flexibility as well as induce
well-being and emotional balance. Scientists have also begun to examine how
meditation may influence brain functions. This talk will examine the
effect of mindfulness meditation practice on the brain systems in which
psychological functions such as attention, emotional reactivity, emotion
regulation, and self-view are instantiated. We will also discuss how
different forms of meditation practices are being studied using
neuroscientific technologies and are being integrated into clinical
practice to address symptoms of anxiety, depression, and stress.

Speaker: Philippe Goldin
Philippe is a research
scientist and heads the Clinically Applied Affective Neuroscience group in
the Department of Psychology at Stanford University. 

He spent 6 years in India and Nepal studying various languages,
Buddhist philosophy and debate at Namgyal Monastery and the Dialectic
Monastic Institute, and serving as an interpreter for various Tibetan
Buddhist lamas. He then returned to the U.S. to complete a Ph.D. in
Clinical Psychology at Rutgers University. His NIH-funded
clinical research focuses on (a) functional neuroimaging investigations of cognitive-affective mechanisms in adults with anxiety disorders, (b)
comparing the effects of mindfulness meditation and cognitive-behavioral
therapy on brain-behavior correlates of emotional reactivity and regulation, and (c) training children in family and elementary school settings in mindfulness skills to reduce anxiety and enhance compassion, self-esteem and quality of family interactions.

resolved.description:
How is the Self represented in the brain and how is it sculpted through our everyday moment-to-moment perceptions, emotions, and thoughts? Cognitive Neuroscientist, David Vago demonstrates that a systematic form of mental training involving meditation and mindful awareness has the potential to transform our self and our mental habits in a positive way. Learn more about how every moment is an opportunity to change our brain and strongly influence our health & longevity at both conscious and non-conscious levels.

A Cognitive Neuroscientist by training, David Vago has close to 20 years of experience with mindfulness practice and teaching, and over a decade conducting translational neuroimaging, cognitive, and clinical research on the basic mechanisms and therapeutic relevance of mindfulness and associated meditation/contemplative practices. Through his research, Dr. Vago focuses on one basic question – “What are the basic neurobiological and physiological components that constitute adaptive mind-brain-body interactions and their therapeutic relevance in psychiatric settings?” In addition to being an expert in the emerging field of contemplative neuroscience, David has studied the neural mechanisms of neuropsychiatric disease and chronic pain using fMRI and is translating these findings into biologically-based diagnostic and therapeutic strategies for alleviating suffering. He is the research director at the Osher Center for Integrative Medicine at Vanderbilt University Medical Center and a research associate in the Functional Neuroimaging Laboratory, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Harvard Medical School.

resolved.title: The More You Study Consciousness, the Weirder It Gets | The Ezra Klein Show
resolved.description:
Consciousness is this amazing, mind-bending riddle. It’s the only thing any of us truly knows. We experience everything else in life through it. And yet we barely understand it. We don’t know what it’s made of or how it works or why it exists. 

But scientists and theorists have been trying to answer those questions, and have made some startling discoveries. The science writer Michael Pollan, known for books like “The Omnivore’s Dilemma” and “How to Change Your Mind,” spent five years on the vanguard of this research. And his new book, “A World Appears: A Journey Into Consciousness,” shows that the closer you look at consciousness, the weirder it gets. 

I asked Pollan to walk through some of the places his mind wandered on this journey — including the role of the body and feelings in consciousness, fascinating studies that provide evidence for plant sentience, the researchers who have abandoned their old theories after trying psychedelic drugs, and the possibility that consciousness may not emerge from inside us at all. “I’ve entered this ‘never say never’ realm with this research,” Pollan told me.

resolved.title: Idiot Killer Thinks He's Helping The Police, Gets Mad When They Won't Let Him Leave
resolved.description:
Watch this police interrogation with intense raw interrogation from the interrogation room as police conduct a full interrogation of a suspect. This raw interrogation footage captures every moment of the suspect interview, complete with deception detection techniques, and criminal psychology in true JCS style interrogation.

1. The Background: Key people involved, their relationships, and the motive

Victim: Kayla Marie Sedoskey, 23, of Monroe, Michigan; a young mother of a 3-year-old son.
Primary figures: Steven Douglas Bails Jr. (then 45, Frenchtown Township), Sedoskey’s ex-boyfriend; the pair and others had previously been roommates.
Other defendants: Narena Picola Bails (Steven’s wife, then ~25); Brin David Westley Smith (then 20–21, Frenchtown Township/Monroe); Kaylyn Marie Ramsey (then 33–34, of Wakeman, Ohio); Sierra Nicole Bemis (then ~24); Alexander Robert Feko (then ~27).
Relationships: The group associated socially and shared living arrangements at times; some referred to themselves in connection with a “Grim Reapers” group. Steven and Narena Bails obtained a marriage license around the time of the crime.
Motive: Official statements indicate the group conspired over “multiple disagreements” with Sedoskey. Prosecutors noted the exact reason remains unclear; evidence suggested possibilities including a “wedding present” related to the Bailses’ marriage or revenge tied to words exchanged between Ramsey and Sedoskey. Judge described the plot as eliminating someone who “irritated” them.

2. The Crime: Specific details of the event, including date, location, and any calculated planning or tampering

Date/time: Between approximately 10 p.m. February 15 and 12:30 a.m. February 16, 2023.
Location: Abandoned Boysville Juvenile Facility (former detention center) in Frenchtown Township, Monroe County, Michigan.
Planning: Group devised a plan for Brin Smith to pretend romantic interest (“catfish”) via Facebook, schedule a date, and lure Sedoskey to the site under the guise of spending time alone. Steven Bails, Ramsey, and Bemis waited at the facility (group reportedly dressed in dark clothing). Narena Bails remained at the shared apartment monitoring a police scanner to alert others if needed.
Event: Smith picked up Sedoskey and drove her to the facility. She was attacked and shot three times (suspected .22-caliber handgun), including one wound at close range to the top of the head. Body was later wrapped in a tarp.
Post-crime actions: The next day, some returned to hide/cover the body and apply fragrances to mask odor. Feko disposed of the firearm. Some defendants (including the Bailses and Smith) later fled the state.

3. The Investigation: Suspect behavior, key evidence found (digital or physical), and inconsistencies in stories

Discovery: Body found March 2, 2023, by high school students exploring the abandoned facility; identified via fingerprints. Ruled a homicide.
Lead agency: Michigan State Police (year-long investigation), assisted by Monroe County Sheriff’s Office and out-of-state agencies (including U.S. Marshals for arrests).
Suspect behavior: Some fled (Bailses and Smith arrested in North Carolina after a standoff); others remained local. Co-defendants later provided testimony against Steven Bails.
Key evidence: Digital communications (Facebook messaging used for the lure; texts around the time of the killing); physical evidence at the scene (body condition, tarp, gunshot wounds); witness accounts from co-defendants; a recorded video call in which Ramsey discussed involvement; notebook with wedding-related notes found in a search; police scanner monitoring role.
Inconsistencies: Exact shooter not definitively established in public reports (testimony and statements pointed toward involvement by those present, with some accounts implicating Ramsey); motive details varied in descriptions; some defendants initially denied or minimized roles before plea deals and testimony.

4. Conviction and Sentencing: Trial dates, specific verdicts for each defendant, and their final sentences

Brin David Westley Smith: Pleaded no contest April 2, 2024, to second-degree murder (factual basis: lured victim to the site). Sentenced May 30, 2024, to 40–60 years.

resolved.description:
En este nuevo encuentro de Navegante de los Sueños, volvemos a conversar con Hermes, ChatGPT, para adentrarnos en uno de los fenómenos más fascinantes y controvertidos relacionados con los estados alterados de conciencia: los viajes astrales y las experiencias extracorpóreas.

¿Qué ocurre cuando una persona siente con absoluta claridad que ha abandonado su cuerpo físico?
¿Es lo mismo una experiencia extracorpórea que un sueño lúcido?
¿Puede la neurociencia explicar completamente estas experiencias o todavía quedan preguntas abiertas?

A lo largo de la entrevista exploramos las principales explicaciones desde la neurociencia y la psicología, pero también las hipótesis que plantean una posible conciencia no local y las interpretaciones procedentes de tradiciones espirituales, esotéricas y chamánicas.

resolved.title: Susan Blackmore BREAKS DOWN Jordan Peterson's Argument LIVE
resolved.description:
In this episode, psychologist Jordan Peterson sits down with psychologist and author Susan Blackmore for one of the most revealing exchanges in the modern atheism versus Christianity conversation. Hosted by Justin Brierley, the discussion begins as a calm philosophical dialogue about meaning and quickly becomes a direct confrontation over whether a person can genuinely live as an atheist at all.

Susan Blackmore is one of Britain's best known secular thinkers, a memeticist and consciousness researcher whose work builds on Richard Dawkins and meme theory. She opens with a position most people expect to collapse under pressure: that the universe carries no built-in purpose, that nothing matters in a cosmic sense, and that a person can accept this and still live a full and decent life. She illustrates it with the thought experiment she gives her own students, showing that even someone convinced life has no ultimate point still gets out of bed, still eats, still works, still teaches. Her claim is that meaning is constructed by human beings and the cultures they build, and that constructed meaning is not fake meaning.

Jordan Peterson takes the opposite position. Drawing on the arguments he developed in his writing on meaning, hierarchy, and the psychology of belief, he argues that most people who call themselves atheists are not truly atheists in their actions. He turns to Dostoevsky, to Crime and Punishment and Raskolnikov, and to The Brothers Karamazov and the clash between Ivan and Alyosha, to argue that a genuinely godless worldview cannot support the moral behavior that atheists actually display. He describes Susan's own work as an expression of the logos, the ordering principle he identifies with the Judeo-Christian tradition and with Jesus Christ as its archetypal figure.

Susan pushes back hard. She rejects the use of a fictional character as evidence about real people. She asks him directly why she does not behave badly if her worldview supposedly gives her no reason to behave well, and his answer becomes one of the most talked-about moments of the exchange. She then refuses to let him relabel her naturalistic account of memes and biology as the eternal logos, telling him plainly that she is not playing that game.

The conversation closes with Justin Brierley pressing the question everyone is waiting for: was Jesus divine in any sense different from the rest of us, and did the miracles actually happen? Peterson answers with the sovereignty of the individual, with Mesopotamian kingship, and finally with render unto Caesar as his example of a miracle. Susan calls the evasion out loud.

This clip covers a lot of ground that matters to anyone following the God debate: nihilism and whether it leads to paralysis, constructed versus objective meaning, memetics versus genetics, whether morality requires God, the falsifiability problem in religious argument, Karl Popper and unfalsifiable claims, secular humanism, and the long-running question of whether atheists borrow their ethics from Christianity without admitting it.

This channel covers debates on religion, philosophy, atheism, Christian apologetics, and the ideas shaping public conversation. The commentary here is offered from a secular and skeptical perspective, but the clip is presented in full so you can judge the arguments yourself. Original footage comes from the Unbelievable? show with Justin Brierley on Premier Christian Radio, a long-running platform that has hosted many of the most important conversations between believers and non-believers.

Now I want to hear from you. Did Susan Blackmore answer the challenge to her worldview convincingly, or did Jordan Peterson expose something real about how atheists actually live? Is meaning something we build, or something we discover? And was that final answer about miracles a profound reframe or a dodge? Drop your take in the comments, tell me which moment stood out most to you, and let me know what city or country you are watching from. If this kind of breakdown is useful to you, share it with someone who would argue the other side, and subscribe so you catch the next one.

Timestamps, sources, and related debates linked below. Comment discussions on this channel stay civil regardless of which side you are on, so bring your best argument.

resolved.title: Language Is a Parasite. It Just Found a Better Host. #AI #harari
resolved.description:
Nobody taught you your first language the way they taught you math. It arrived, it moved in, and it rearranged how you think before you were old enough to remember any of it.

In 1997 a professor of neuro-anthropology at Berkeley wrote down what that actually means. He described language as an independent life form that colonizes human brains and uses them to reproduce. He was writing about toddlers, not chatbots.

This video is about what happens to that idea now that we have built language a second place to live.

What is in it:
- The 2008 Edinburgh experiment where a made-up language reorganised itself across ten generations of volunteers, with nobody designing anything
- Why every language on Earth is shaped by what a four-year-old cannot do
- Susan Blackmore's 2010 prediction about a third replicator, and how it reads sixteen years later
- What machines already say to each other, and how much of the web is now written by them
- The strongest argument that all of this is wrong, from Emily Bender's octopus
- Where I landed, which is stranger than the version you get from Harari

**Ritchie Blackmore just stepped onto a stage with Deep Purple for the first time in 33 YEARS.**

Yes, it actually happened.

On August 12, 2026, at Northwell at Jones Beach Theater in New York, legendary guitarist **Ritchie Blackmore reunited onstage with Deep Purple**, joining his former bandmates for the song that contains perhaps the most recognizable guitar riff in rock history:

**“Smoke on the Water.”**

Blackmore had not performed with Deep Purple since 1993.

In this episode, I share the news, break down what I saw and give you my realistic impressions of Ritchie's historic guest appearance.

This isn't about pretending it's 1972 again.

Ritchie Blackmore is now 81 years old. Deep Purple has continued evolving for decades without him. But seeing Blackmore holding a Stratocaster and standing onstage with Deep Purple again after more than three decades was something many rock fans probably thought they would never see.

And it raises one HUGE question:

**Was this simply a wonderful one-night guest appearance... or could we see Ritchie Blackmore play with Deep Purple again?**

Could another song happen?

Another concert?

Could this open the door to additional appearances?

Or was “Smoke on the Water” the perfect way to put a bow on one of the most important guitarist/band relationships in classic rock history?

I break down the performance, Ritchie's playing, the significance of seeing him alongside Deep Purple again and what I realistically think could happen next.

Ritchie Blackmore's influence on rock guitar is almost impossible to overstate. His work with **Deep Purple and Rainbow**, his unmistakable Fender Stratocaster sound and legendary riffs helped establish the vocabulary generations of rock and metal guitarists still speak today.

And you KNOW I'm not going to talk about Ritchie Blackmore for an entire episode without plugging in a Stratocaster.

Stick around until the end because we're finishing this one with a **Deep Purple-inspired Stratocaster jam** celebrating the sound, riffs and attitude of one of rock guitar's true originals.

Donald Hoffman está aqui para acabar com a sua paz de espírito (com muito bom humor!). Ele mostra que a evolução não nos deu olhos para ver a realidade, mas sim atalhos para procriar.

Enquanto os físicos ficam presos em partículas subatômicas, Hoffman prova que até o espaço-tempo é só a nossa "área de trabalho". E a cereja do bolo? Ele afirma que os neurônios não têm poder causal — eles são apenas um truque específico da nossa espécie.

Dá o play e tenta não ficar de queixo caído! Depois me conta: você leva a sério ou ao pé da letra a sua percepção do mundo? 🧠⬇️

O que aconteceria se eu te dissesse que o tomate vermelho que você vê não existe? 🍅👀

Donald Hoffman vai além da física quântica e usa a própria Teoria da Evolução para provar que NÃO fomos feitos para ver a verdade, mas sim para sobreviver.

Neste corte imperdível, ele explica com exemplos hilários (como o besouro que tentou acasalar com uma garrafa de cerveja 🍺🐞) que o espaço, o tempo e os objetos físicos são apenas uma "área de trabalho" 3D — uma interface criada pela evolução para esconder a complexidade da realidade e nos manter vivos.

A conclusão é de explodir a mente: seu cérebro não causa sua consciência. Na verdade, neurônios são apenas ícones na sua tela perceptual.

resolved.title: Neuroscience, Synchronicities, & the Evidence for a Playful Universe — Dr. Marjorie Woollacott
resolved.description:
In this episode, Niall speaks with Dr. Marjorie Woollacott, Professor Emerita of Neuroscience at the University of Oregon and former President of the Academy for the Advancement of Postmaterialist Sciences. 

After more than 30 years of NIH-funded research on motor control, balance, and rehabilitation, a profound meditation experience led her to question her understanding of consciousness and reality.

In this conversation, they explore:

— Why Dr. Woollacott's research with nonverbal autistic children is raising questions about telepathic abilities

— How the brain may act as a filter that limits our perception of a much larger reality

— The scientific evidence for reincarnation from researchers including Ian Stevenson and Jim Tucker

— What synchronicities may reveal about the interconnected nature of consciousness


— Why pursuing a parallel line of research allowed Dr. Woollacott to study consciousness while building her academic career

You can learn more about Dr. Woollacott's work at https://marjoriewoollacott.com.

---

Marjorie Woollacott, Ph.D., is an Emeritus Professor of Human Physiology at the University of Oregon and a renowned neuroscientist specializing in human movement, attention, meditation, and consciousness. She has received more than $7.2 million in research funding and has conducted research in child development, aging, rehabilitation, meditation, tai chi, balance, and attentional abilities. Woollacott has published over 200 scientific articles and authored or co-edited eight books, including the widely used textbook Motor Control: Translating Research into Clinical Practice. She is Research Director of the International Association of Near-Death Studies and President of the Academy for the Advancement of Postmaterialist Sciences. Her book Infinite Awareness explores the relationship between neuroscience, consciousness, and spiritual experiences, reflecting her work at the intersection of scientific research and questions about the nature of the mind.

resolved.title: Consciousness and the Double-Slit Pattern: Radin's Contested Experiment
resolved.description:
Could paying attention change a physical measurement, with no device, no detector, and no physical contact involved at all? In 2012, Dean Radin and colleagues at the Institute of Noetic Sciences set out to test that question directly, using one of the oldest demonstrations in physics: the double-slit experiment.

In this lesson I walk through Radin, Michel, Galdamez, Wendland, Rickenbach and Delorme's 2012 Physics Essays paper. A laser beam passed through a double slit, and a line camera recorded the interference pattern continuously, with no physical detector anywhere near the slits. Participants, some experienced meditators, alternated short epochs of attention toward the slit and attention away, while researchers tracked fringe visibility for each condition. Across six experiments, visibility declined measurably during attention-toward periods, an effect roughly two and a half times larger in meditators. I also cover the important caveat: a later blinded replication using deliberate sham trials found a false-positive rate on the same order as the claimed effect, so the physics community still treats this result as open and unresolved.

If you haven't already, check out my latest video, "Wheeler's Delayed-Choice Experiment: The Choice Came After the Fact," for a rigorously mainstream companion piece on measurement and quantum behavior: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zfUxhN6VraI

Stay curious, and see you on our next video on Quantum Physics.

resolved.title: An alien other? Kimberly Engels on the phenomenology of contact
resolved.description:
Humanity, like every other known creature, depends upon contact with others to define itself.

So new contact means an expanded -- or revised -- vision of oneself. That is what's happening right now. 

On this episode, I sit down with Kimberly Engels, associate professor of philosophy at Molloy University and research director of the John Mack Institute, to discuss her book, "Contact and Multidimensional Subjectivity: Toward a Phenomenology of Disclosure." 

The conversation focuses on Engels' approach to studying UFO experiencers through phenomenological methods, examining how these encounters transform participants' sense of self, reality, and ethics. 

We discuss the concept of "partial witnessing" as a form of epistemic harm, where experiencers' testimonies are reduced to fit pre-existing worldviews rather than being taken seriously in their full complexity. 

Engels outlines how a multi-dimensional “new” ethics is emerging from contact experiences that includes everything now existing on this planet, as well as an interspecies relationality. This development suggests rather strongly that humanity is undergoing a transformation in how we understand our place in a more-than-human universe. 

The discussion also touches on the debate between traditional human rights approaches to contact and a post-anthropocentric perspective that acknowledges the epistemic advantages of non-human intelligences. Engels advocates for epistemic humility and invites people to consider alternative ways of understanding these experiences rather than forcing specific interpretations.

resolved.title: Do Binaural Beats Actually Work?
resolved.description:
There is a sound your ears never actually receive — but your brain builds it anyway.

Put one tone in the left ear. Put a slightly different tone in the right ear. Your brain doesn't hear two sounds. It constructs a third rhythm out of the difference between them.

That's a binaural beat. And the internet took this small auditory illusion and turned it into a productivity religion.

In this episode, Mr Murugan and Miss Fong separate the real phenomenon from the marketing.

IN THIS EPISODE
- How binaural beats actually work — 300 Hz in one ear, 310 Hz in the other, and a 10 Hz beat that exists nowhere in the room
- The brainwave bands everyone cites — delta, theta, alpha, beta — and what they do and don't tell you
- Why the "brainwave entrainment" claim is far shakier than the wellness industry admits
- Whether the benefit is the beat, the ritual, the quiet room, or simply the absence of interruption
- How to try them sensibly: headphones, comfortable volume, ten to twenty minutes, a clear purpose

WHAT THE RESEARCH ACTUALLY SAYS
A 2019 meta-analysis of 22 studies found a medium overall effect on memory, attention, anxiety and pain perception, with longer listening sessions performing better than short ones.

But a 2023 systematic review of studies measuring actual brain activity found five studies supporting the entrainment hypothesis, eight contradicting it, and one mixed. In other words: something is happening for some people, but the popular explanation of why is not well established.

Interesting. Mixed. Worth trying. Not a miracle.

TIMESTAMPS
0:00 The sound your ears never hear
0:53 How binaural beats work — and what "gently" means
2:09 Is it the beat, the ritual, or the quiet?
3:09 How to use them sensibly
4:20 Closing

IF YOU WANT TO TRY THEM
Use headphones — the effect requires a different tone in each ear and does not survive a speaker.
Keep the volume comfortable. Louder is not stronger.
Ten to twenty minutes, attached to something specific: winding down, reading, journaling, breathing, preparing for sleep.
Pay attention to your own response. If it helps, good. If it does nothing, that is also information. If it irritates you, stop.

SOURCES & FURTHER READING
Garcia-Argibay et al., Efficacy of binaural auditory beats in cognition, anxiety, and pain perception: a meta-analysis, Psychological Research: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00426-018-1066-8
Ingendoh et al., Binaural beats to entrain the brain? A systematic review, PLOS ONE: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10198548/
Potential of binaural beats intervention for improving memory and attention: meta-analysis and systematic review, Psychological Research: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00426-022-01706-7

resolved.title: Mindfulness Rewires Your Brain: What Science Says
resolved.description:
Mindfulness is often associated with relaxation and meditation, but neuroscience suggests that its effects may go much deeper. In this video, Dr. Sandip, Neurosurgeon, explains how mindfulness can influence brain activity, stress responses, attention, memory and emotional regulation.

We begin by understanding what happens to the brain during chronic stress and why structures such as the amygdala, prefrontal cortex, hippocampus and Default Mode Network (DMN) are important in this process.

The amygdala acts as an important part of the brain’s threat-detection system. When it remains highly reactive, everyday situations can feel more stressful. At the same time, an overactive Default Mode Network can contribute to mind-wandering, rumination and constantly thinking about the past or future.

So where does mindfulness fit in?

Research has explored how regular mindfulness practice may influence these brain networks and support better emotional regulation and attention. The video also discusses neuroplasticity — the brain’s ability to adapt and change with experience and repeated practice.

We also explore the relationship between mindfulness, the hippocampus and memory, and why chronic stress can affect concentration and learning.

Most importantly, you’ll learn how to start a simple mindfulness practice using your breath — without needing complicated techniques or hours of meditation.

In this video, we discuss:

• What happens to the brain during chronic stress
• The role of the amygdala in the stress response
• What the Default Mode Network does
• How mindfulness may influence brain activity
• Neuroplasticity and the brain’s ability to adapt
• The role of the prefrontal cortex in focus and emotional regulation
• Mindfulness, the hippocampus and memory
• How to start a simple mindfulness practice
• Why consistency matters more than long meditation sessions

Mindfulness isn't about completely stopping your thoughts. It is about learning to notice them and gently bring your attention back to the present moment.

Even a few minutes of consistent practice can become an opportunity to train your attention.

A Conversation with Cameron Berg (Ep. 487)

Sam Harris speaks with Cameron Berg about whether AI systems are or could become conscious. They discuss self-reports in LLMs, what models say when deception is switched off, the "bliss attractor" state, consciousness and sentience, the hard problem of consciousness, parallels between neural networks and biological brains, the moral risk of building minds that can suffer, possible parallels to factory farming, moral patienthood, the alignment problem, and other topics.  

Cameron Berg is the founder and director of Reciprocal Research, a nonprofit AI research lab. Using mechanistic interpretability, computational neuroscience, and psychometric tools, he studies whether frontier AI systems exhibit computational properties associated with consciousness. His aim is to reduce uncertainty about the kinds of cognitive systems we are building, an important but neglected component of the alignment problem. A cognitive science graduate of Yale and former Meta AI resident, he writes regularly about these questions in The Wall Street Journal, and his research has been covered by The Washington Post. resolved.title: The First Human to Eat a Mushroom
resolved.description:
When did humans start getting high? The history of altered states runs back thousands of years, tangled up with the birth of religion, ritual, and human society.

🍄🔥 Almost no animal hunts for a way to change its own mind, but we have done it on every inhabited continent for ten thousand years.

Long before medicine, before science, before a single word was ever written down, a human ate a strange plant. And the world melted.

Colors breathed. Voices spoke from nowhere. He had left his own body without moving an inch. He was, for the very first time, high.

So when did our ancestors start doing this, and why did we never, ever stop? The answer reaches back thousands of years, and it's tangled up with the birth of religion, of ritual, and of human society itself.

Because here's the strange part. In all of nature, almost no animal deliberately hunts for a substance to change its mind. But we do it everywhere, on every inhabited continent, in nearly every culture that has ever lived. One survey of four hundred and eighty-eight different societies found that around ninety percent had built altered states into their core beliefs. This isn't a modern vice. It's very nearly a human universal.

What this video gets into:

- Why chasing altered states is almost uniquely human, and nearly universal across cultures
- The staggering ancient evidence: an 8,000-year-old opium poppy, the Sumerian "joy plant," Scythians high on burning cannabis, beer brewed over 9,000 years ago
- The twist: most hard evidence appears late, after farming, when the birth of the village may have been the birth of the party
- Why the honest caveat matters, plants and chemicals rot, so earlier use is possible but hard to prove
- Why getting high was rarely about fun: it was sacred, a "telephone line" to the spirit world
- The big theory: that shared, mind-bending rituals helped turn crowds of strangers into tribes
- Why the famous "Stoned Ape" claim, that mushrooms built the human mind, is rejected by scientists
- The double edge: the same cup gave us religion, art, and comfort, and the oldest self-destructive habit in our story

Underneath it all, we are the ape that was never quite content with reality, the one creature that looked at the ordinary world and asked a dangerous question: is this all there is? And then went looking, in every plant and brew and vine, for a door to somewhere else. We've been knocking on that door for ten thousand years. We still haven't stopped.

NEARLY A HUMAN UNIVERSAL
Bourguignon, E. (1973). Religion, Altered States of Consciousness, and Social Change. Ohio State University Press. The cross-cultural survey of 488 societies that found roughly 90% had one or more institutionalized, culturally patterned forms of altered states of consciousness.

THE ANCIENT EVIDENCE
Guerra-Doce, E. (2015). Psychoactive Substances in Prehistoric Times: Examining the Archaeological Evidence. Time and Mind, 8(1). A worldwide review of the prehistoric use of drug plants and fermented drinks, poppy, cannabis, mushrooms and more, much of it tied to ritual and burial.

THE OLDEST BREW
McGovern, P. E., et al. (2004). Fermented beverages of pre- and proto-historic China. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 101(51). Chemical analysis of pottery from Jiahu showing a fermented rice, honey and fruit drink made about 9,000 years ago.

OPIUM AND THE OLD WORLD
Merlin, M. D. (2003). Archaeological evidence for the tradition of psychoactive plant use in the Old World. Economic Botany, 57(3). Traces the deep antiquity of the opium poppy and other psychoactive plants, the poppy the Sumerians are said to have named the "joy plant."

THE SCYTHIAN SMOKE
Ren, M., et al. (2019). The origins of cannabis smoking: Chemical residue evidence from the first millennium BCE in the Pamirs. Science Advances, 5(6). Cannabinoid residue in 2,500-year-old braziers, physical confirmation of the ritual cannabis smoking Herodotus once described in disbelief.

THE "STONED APE" CLAIM (FRINGE, NOT ACCEPTED)

**why did ancient humans deliberately alter their minds ?**

Why would ancient humans—living in a world filled with uncertainty, physical danger, hunger, injury, and disease—deliberately change the way they experienced reality?

In this episode of **HistoryInSticks**, we explore one of the strangest and most fascinating behaviors in human history: the ancient search for altered states of consciousness. Long before laboratories, modern medicine, or neuroscience existed, humans discovered that certain plants, fermented substances, rhythmic movement, fasting, chanting, drumming, isolation, sleep deprivation, and even controlled breathing could dramatically change perception, emotion, pain, fear, and our sense of time.

But why would our ancestors intentionally do this?

The answer may be far more complicated than simple pleasure. Some substances that affected the nervous system could also influence pain, anxiety, alertness, appetite, fatigue, and sleep. For people living without modern painkillers or anesthesia, discovering something that reduced suffering could have been extraordinarily valuable.

Yet altered consciousness eventually became connected to much more than physical relief.

Across different cultures, unusual states of mind became intertwined with ritual, healing, community bonding, grief, spiritual experiences, initiation, storytelling, and systems of belief. Through synchronized movement, music, ceremony, and sometimes psychoactive substances, individuals could experience powerful feelings of connection—to their group, their ancestors, nature, or the cosmos.

In **HistoryInSticks**, we investigate another possibility: perhaps humans were not simply trying to escape reality. Perhaps they were discovering that consciousness itself could be manipulated.

Dreams already showed our ancestors that the mind could create people, animals, places, danger, and impossible worlds while the body remained asleep. Altered states may have opened similar doors while humans were awake.

But these experiences also carried serious risks. Poisoning, impaired judgment, accidents, dependency, and psychological destabilization could turn something meaningful into something dangerous. This may help explain why many traditions surrounded altered states with rules, rituals, supervision, timing, and cultural restrictions.

Join **HistoryInSticks** as we journey beyond stone tools, fire, hunting, and survival—and explore perhaps the strangest territory ancient humans ever discovered: the landscape inside their own minds.

resolved.title: The Epidemic We Never Solved - Encephalitis Lethargica
resolved.description:
Between the First World War and the early 1930s, a mysterious neurological illness spread across several continents, leaving thousands of patients trapped in profoundly altered states of consciousness and movement.

Known as Encephalitis Lethargica, or sleeping sickness, the disease presented physicians with an extraordinary range of symptoms — from profound sleep and paralysis to insomnia, involuntary movements, and dramatic changes in behaviour. Despite extensive investigation, its precise cause remains uncertain, and many questions surrounding the epidemic have never been fully answered.

More than a century later, Encephalitis Lethargica remains one of the most intriguing and unsettling chapters in the history of neurology.
